segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: To do, or to make, in Spanish is hacer, and it has a silent H. It's h-a-c-e-r.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, in most of Spain, actually, that would sound hacer. But hacer in most of the Spanish speaking world. What verb type is it? What is the ending?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: -er.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: -er verb. So, actually, whenever we come across a new verb, we want to make a mental note: what is the ending? Or rather than make a mental note, just process it. Remember, we always want to do anything but memorize. So, just looking and going, hacer, -er verb. Okay. Just to get in that habit.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: If we know it's an -er verb, we know how to work with it. So, how would you say: he's doing or making; she is doing or making; you are, formal, doing or making?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Hace.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Hace. Good. You're doing it?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Lo hace.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Lo hace. How would you say they're doing it, or you guys are doing it?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Los hacen. Lo hacen.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. Very good. Lo hacen.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: You, informal, are doing it. So what is the sound for informal you?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Hacen.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So for informal you, we add on an S to the he/she/it version. So we get...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Haces.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Haces. You're doing it?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Lo haces.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. The word for what in Spanish is qué. How would you say what are you doing?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ¿Qué haces?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: ¿Qué haces? And this is a way of saying how are you as well. ¿Qué haces?, what are you doing?, what are you up to? Good. So,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: we see that for -ar verbs, we have the principal sound of a, and then we add our N or S: N for they or you plural, and S for informal you.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And for -er/-ir verbs, we have the key sound e, and we're adding on S for informal you, N for they, you plural. Now, these associations

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: between -s and informal you, and -n and they or you guys, we're going to see all throughout the Spanish verb structure.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: So, I'm This confuses me a little bit. Isn't this also a memorization? Having to remember which ending goes with what

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: people. There's a difference between memorization and remembering. Ah? We're going to remember through not actively trying to memorize.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, I'm not telling you you shouldn't remember anything, you need to remember Spanish. I'm telling you that you're going to remember it much easier without that active process of trying to memorize anything, which blocks

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: whichever processes we need for remembering. I like to describe it in this way: that you borrow information when you memorize it,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: but when you are applying it practically in this construction of these sentences, when you are looking from many different angles at the elements that we're looking at in Spanish, then you are internalizing it. Then it's really yours, you're not borrowing it.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Puedo, puedo in Spanish means I can, I am able. Puedo.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Puedo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. P-u-e-d-o. Puedo.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Puedo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: You're probably noticing as well that the D is quite soft when it comes in the middle of a word in Spanish rather than a hard d. Puedo.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Puedo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, puedo means I can or I am able, and the to-form of the verb is an -er verb.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, puedo is an -er verb. So, how would you say he can, or she can, or it can, or you, formal, can?

segments.speaker: Student

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Puede. And how would you say informally, you can?

segments.speaker: Student

segments.text: Good. Now, in English, we don't say can you to come? But, it's what we mean. Now, this is an English problem. English is taking the to away here. It does it sometimes.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: You don't say I must to come, you say I must come, no? It's like I am able to come, you can think of it this way, as we thought of I must come as I owe to come. So, how would you say can you come?, talking informally.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Puede... sorry, informal, ¿puedes venir?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: ¿Puedes venir? So this is what we're going to be using to talk with friends, you know, this S. We're going to be hearing it a lot. If it helps to make the association, you might have heard ¿cómo estás?, how are you? The S on the end of estás

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: there, is this informal S. Puedes. So, can't you come?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ¿No puedes venir?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: ¿No puedes venir? Why can't you come?

segments.speaker: Student

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: ¿Por qué no puedes venir? I want to know why you can't come.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Quiero... oh, to know, um. Okay, I'm doing know, knowledge, and that's not taking me anywhere.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Boy's got savvy.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Ah, yes.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, I want to know?

segments.speaker: Student

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Quiero saber. Why?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Por qué.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: You can't come?

segments.speaker: Student

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. Very good. If we address each part, part by part, and apply all of our mental energy just to the part we need, and then forget it. Quiero saber por qué no puedes venir. Very good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, to recap: we have -ar verbs, and we have -er/-ir verbs.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: For all of the verbs, we take off the ending, -ar, -er, -ir, and we put -o for the I-version.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, vender is to sell, and I sell is?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Vendo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Vendo. Comprar is to buy, and I buy is?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Compro.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Compro, good. Llegar is, er, to arrive, llegar, and I arrive is?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Llegaro. Lle... oh, llego.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Llego. Good. So with this rule, we can take any verb and we can do this. If it's regular. Maybe it's irregular, and we try it and we make a mistake. So for example, salir is to leave or to go out.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: If we apply this rule, what are we going to come up with?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Salo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Salo. But it's wrong, it's salgo. So it's one of those -go instead of -o, like vengo, I'm coming,

segments.speaker: Student

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: tengo, I have, salgo, I leave, I'm going out. They're quite common verbs. We tend to find in all languages that the most common verbs are the most irregular.

segments.text: Esperar, esperar means to wait and to hope.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Which is interesting, and it's accurate enough. I mean, you're not doing much more than waiting when you hope.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We have it in the word desperate, actually. Des- is un-, and you're hopeless when you're desperate.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, esperar is to wait or to hope. How do you say I'm waiting, or I'm hoping, or I wait, or I hope?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Espero.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Espero. Now, how do you say he waits?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Eh, esp... espere.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: I'm really glad you made that mistake, actually, because it's a it's a wonderful point to elaborate on.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Before we touch a verb, we want to take one split second to go: esperar, -ar verb.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Otherwise, what happens? Our brain hears e, e from esperar, and it wants to put an e.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What your mind is doing there, putting an E because you have es-pe- and it fits better, is actually even ingrained in in other languages. For example, in Turkish you have something called vowel harmony,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: and when you're adding on suffixes, there's like two or four, depending on the suffix, two or four different versions of that suffix that you can add on, so it can agree with the vowel before.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, there's something in your mind that would prefer an E there, of course, because it's es-pe-.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And like I said, you even see this formalized in other languages, like in this phenomenon of vowel harmony.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, to stop that process from happening, you must run back to the to-form, and then you take control.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Espera.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Espera. And espera means he, she, it, you formal, wait or are waiting, is waiting. We can build the rest. So, how do you say they wait?

segments.text: If you want to say they're waiting for me, we don't need the word for for. It's just like they await me. We don't need the word for for. So, how do you say they await me?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Esperan me... sorry, me esperan.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Me esperan. The only option there, because it's a changed verb: me esperan. They're not waiting for me?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No me esperan.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. No me esperan. I want to know why they're not waiting for me. I want to know?

segments.text: Why?

segments.speaker: Student

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. Quiero saber por qué no me esperan. Well done.
